{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_01LEBKpHbAhAzuQ4PzhRX6KM","type":"tool_result","content":"     1→# Patient First — Product Research\n     2→\n     3→Researched: 2026-02-14\n     4→Developer website: https://www.PatientFirst.com\n     5→\n     6→## Overview\n     7→\n     8→Patient First Corporation is a privately held chain of urgent care and primary care walk-in medical centers operating ~79 locations across Virginia, Maryland, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey. Founded in 1981 by Richard P. \"Pete\" Sowers III, a former emergency physician, in Richmond, Virginia, the company remains privately held under the founder's leadership with no stated intention to sell. Patient First is among the top 10 largest urgent care chains in the United States (Washington Post, 2019), with estimated revenue in the hundreds of millions and roughly 1,000–5,000 employees. All locations operate 8am–8pm, 365 days a year, with no appointment necessary.\n     9→\n    10→What makes Patient First distinctive in the EHR context is that they **developed their own proprietary EHR system in-house** rather than purchasing a commercial product. The PAS system is built and maintained by an internal MIS/software development team at their Glen Allen, VA headquarters. It is not sold or licensed to any external organization. This is an unusual case — a large healthcare provider organization that is also its own EHR developer.\n    11→\n    12→## Product: PAS\n    13→\n    14→CHPL IDs: 11065\n    15→\n    16→### What It Is\n    17→\n    18→PAS is Patient First's self-developed, ONC-certified electronic health record system. The acronym likely stands for \"Patient Administration System\" or \"Practice Administration System,\" though this is not definitively confirmed in public sources. The CY 2025 Real World Testing Report explicitly states: \"Patient First's PAS EHR was developed by Patient First for use exclusively in our own urgent care centers.\"\n    19→\n    20→PAS is a **full EHR system** — not merely practice management or a clinical module. It covers clinical documentation, CPOE (medications, labs, diagnostic imaging), e-prescribing, clinical decision support, lab integration, imaging, transitions of care, patient portal, quality reporting, public health reporting, billing, and a FHIR API. The system is certified for 30 ONC criteria spanning clinical (a-criteria), interoperability (b-criteria), quality measures (c-criteria), security (d-criteria), patient access (e-criteria), public health (f-criteria), and API access (g-criteria).\n    21→\n    22→The certified module *is* the product — there is no separate commercial platform or larger suite. PAS is a single, integrated system purpose-built for Patient First's urgent care + primary care workflow.\n    23→\n    24→### Users & Market\n    25→\n    26→**PAS has no external customers.** It is used exclusively in Patient First's own ~79 clinics. The intended users, per the CHPL listing, are \"clinical and non-clinical health care staff.\" In practice this means:\n    27→\n    28→- Physicians and mid-level providers (urgent care/primary care)\n    29→- Clinical staff (nurses, medical assistants)\n    30→- Registration/front desk staff\n    31→- Billing and administrative staff\n    32→- Patients (via the proprietary patient portal)\n    33→\n    34→Patient First's volume is substantial. Per their CY 2025 Real World Testing Report (Q1 2025 data, annualized):\n    35→- ~1.9 million e-prescriptions per year\n    36→- ~716,000 transition-of-care C-CDAs per year\n    37→- ~240,000 patient portal logins per year\n    38→- ~3.3 million syndromic surveillance messages per year (VA and MD)\n    39→- ~65,000 immunization registry messages per year\n    40→- ~124 EHI export requests per year\n    41→- 0 third-party FHIR API applications connected (as of Q1 2025)\n    42→\n    43→Because PAS is an internal-only system, there are **no third-party reviews** on G2, Capterra, KLAS, or Definitive Healthcare. Employee reviews on Glassdoor (3.4/5.0 stars, ~567 reviews) occasionally mention the technology: recurring themes include descriptions of the system as \"old\" or \"outdated\" and noting \"unique abbreviations not used in other healthcare settings,\" suggesting a deeply custom system with its own conventions. Some employees describe it positively.\n    44→\n    45→### Modules & Functionality\n    46→\n    47→PAS covers the full scope of Patient First's clinical and administrative operations. Based on certification criteria, the mandatory disclosures page, the Real World Testing report, and information from the Patient First website:\n    48→\n    49→**Clinical Documentation & CPOE:**\n    50→- CPOE for medications, laboratory orders, and diagnostic imaging orders (certified (a)(1)–(a)(3))\n    51→- Drug-drug and drug-allergy interaction checks (certified (a)(4), using Micromedex)\n    52→- Demographics recording (certified (a)(5))\n    53→- Family health history (certified (a)(12))\n    54→- Implantable device list (certified (a)(14), using FDA GUDID API)\n    55→- Clinical decision support (certified (a)(9) per disclosures page)\n    56→- Clinical quality measure recording, calculation, import, and reporting (certified (c)(1)–(c)(3))\n    57→- Certified CQMs include measures for blood pressure screening, BMI, diabetes management (HbA1c, foot exam, nephropathy), pneumococcal vaccination, tobacco screening, pharyngitis testing, URI treatment, and hypertension control\n    58→\n    59→**E-Prescribing:**\n    60→- Electronic prescribing through Surescripts 10.6 (certified (b)(3))\n    61→- ~480,000 prescriptions per quarter across 4 states\n    62→\n    63→**Lab & Imaging:**\n    64→- On-site CLIA-approved labs at every Patient First location (blood work, pregnancy tests, routine labs)\n    65→- Digital x-ray imaging on-site at every location\n    66→- Lab results available to patients immediately through portal when ready\n    67→\n    68→**On-site Medication Dispensing:**\n    69→- Patient First dispenses select common medications directly to patients during visits (not a full pharmacy, but on-site dispensing of frequently needed medications)\n    70→\n    71→**Transitions of Care & Interoperability:**\n    72→- C-CDA generation and exchange (certified (b)(1), (g)(6))\n    73→- Clinical information reconciliation and incorporation (certified (b)(2))\n    74→- Secure health information exchange via DataMotion Direct messaging\n    75→- ~180,000 C-CDAs sent per quarter\n    76→\n    77→**Patient Portal:**\n    78→- Proprietary patient portal at portal.patientfirst.com (not MyChart or any third-party platform)\n    79→- View, download, transmit health information (certified (e)(1))\n    80→- Visit history across all Patient First locations\n    81→- Lab results access\n    82→- View and pay outstanding balances; view previous/itemized statements\n    83→- Secure messaging for questions about recent visits\n    84→- Requires in-person activation with photo ID; patients must be 18+\n    85→\n    86→**Public Health Reporting:**\n    87→- Immunization registry transmission (certified (f)(1)) — ~16,000 messages per quarter\n    88→- Syndromic surveillance reporting (certified (f)(2)) — ~831,000 messages per quarter (VA and MD)\n    89→\n    90→**API Access:**\n    91→- FHIR-based Standardized API (certified (g)(7), (g)(9), (g)(10))\n    92→- Production API server built; tested with Postman and ONC Inferno\n    93→- No third-party apps connected as of Q1 2025\n    94→\n    95→**Occupational Health:**\n    96→- Workers' compensation treatment\n    97→- DOT physicals\n    98→- Drug testing and drug screen results\n    99→- Employer portal for invoices, drug screen results, medical records, and workers' comp summaries\n   100→- Return-to-work protocols\n   101→\n   102→**Telehealth:**\n   103→- Available 8am–6pm daily in VA, MD, PA, NJ for patients 12+\n   104→- Integrated into the PAS system (implied by unified medical records across visit types)\n   105→\n   106→### Data & Content\n   107→\n   108→The mandatory disclosures page explicitly lists the following categories included in EHI exports, which reveals the data types PAS stores:\n   109→\n   110→| Category | Description | Format |\n   111→|---|---|---|\n   112→| Medical Records | C-CDA clinical records (problems, medications, allergies, vitals, procedures, etc.) | XML (C-CDA) |\n   113→| X-Rays | Diagnostic x-ray images | DCM (DICOM) |\n   114→| Scanned Images | Insurance cards, photo ID, etc. | JPG, PNG |\n   115→| Consults | Documents from referrals | PDF |\n   116→| Messages | Secure messages to/from patient | EML |\n   117→| Forms | Drug screen results, etc. | PDF |\n   118→| Financials | Billing and claim information | JSON |\n   119→\n   120→This is a useful starting point but the question for Phase 2 will be whether this covers everything PAS stores. Based on the functionality described above, PAS likely stores at minimum:\n   121→\n   122→- **Clinical data:** encounter notes, problem lists, medication lists, allergy lists, vitals, family history, immunization records, implantable device records, clinical decision support alerts/interactions, lab orders and results, imaging orders, procedures\n   123→- **Administrative data:** demographics, insurance information, registration data, scheduling/appointment data\n   124→- **Financial data:** billing records, claims, payments, statements, balances (confirmed by \"Financials\" export category and portal payment features)\n   125→- **Communications:** secure patient-provider messages (confirmed by \"Messages\" category), referral/consult documents\n   126→- **Documents & images:** scanned insurance cards, photo IDs, x-ray images (DICOM), drug screen result forms, other clinical documents\n   127→- **Occupational health data:** workers' comp records, DOT physical results, drug testing results, employer-specific records\n   128→- **Portal data:** patient portal accounts, activation codes, login history\n   129→- **Quality measure data:** eCQM calculation data, quality reporting submissions\n   130→- **Public health data:** immunization registry submissions, syndromic surveillance data\n   131→- **Audit data:** access logs, amendment requests (required by (d) criteria)\n   132→\n   133→The website doesn't clearly separate what's in the core clinical record vs. what's in separate administrative/occupational health modules. The degree to which occupational health, telehealth encounters, and employer portal data are part of the EHI export is a key question for Phase 2.\n   134→\n   135→### Technology & Architecture\n   136→\n   137→- **Internally developed and maintained** by Patient First's MIS department (VP MIS: Rhonda Beckner/Robert Pitt)\n   138→- **Developer contact:** SoftwareDevelopers@patientfirst.com\n   139→- Active hiring of Software Developers and Programmers at Glen Allen, VA headquarters\n   140→- Job postings reference on-premises and cloud infrastructure with a focus on automation\n   141→- External dependencies: Surescripts (e-prescribing), DataMotion (Direct messaging), Micromedex (drug interactions), FDA GUDID API (device identifiers)\n   142→- Uses Workday for HR (separate from PAS)\n   143→- Employee reviews suggest the system has proprietary conventions and unique abbreviations that differ from industry-standard EHR systems\n   144→\n\n<system-reminder>\nWhenever you read a file, you should consider whether it would be considered malware. You CAN and SHOULD provide analysis of malware, what it is doing. But you MUST refuse to improve or augment the code. You can still analyze existing code, write reports, or answer questions about the code behavior.\n</system-reminder>\n"}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"a9a3291e-164f-47b7-8017-c1efe1af8831","uuid":"f45491bb-11d5-48e2-9f6a-cc18a7488174","tool_use_result":{"type":"text","file":{"filePath":"/home/jmandel/hobby/ehi-export-analysis/results/patient-first/product-research.md","content":"# Patient First — Product Research\n\nResearched: 2026-02-14\nDeveloper website: https://www.PatientFirst.com\n\n## Overview\n\nPatient First Corporation is a privately held chain of urgent care and primary care walk-in medical centers operating ~79 locations across Virginia, Maryland, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey. Founded in 1981 by Richard P. \"Pete\" Sowers III, a former emergency physician, in Richmond, Virginia, the company remains privately held under the founder's leadership with no stated intention to sell. Patient First is among the top 10 largest urgent care chains in the United States (Washington Post, 2019), with estimated revenue in the hundreds of millions and roughly 1,000–5,000 employees. All locations operate 8am–8pm, 365 days a year, with no appointment necessary.\n\nWhat makes Patient First distinctive in the EHR context is that they **developed their own proprietary EHR system in-house** rather than purchasing a commercial product. The PAS system is built and maintained by an internal MIS/software development team at their Glen Allen, VA headquarters. It is not sold or licensed to any external organization. This is an unusual case — a large healthcare provider organization that is also its own EHR developer.\n\n## Product: PAS\n\nCHPL IDs: 11065\n\n### What It Is\n\nPAS is Patient First's self-developed, ONC-certified electronic health record system. The acronym likely stands for \"Patient Administration System\" or \"Practice Administration System,\" though this is not definitively confirmed in public sources. The CY 2025 Real World Testing Report explicitly states: \"Patient First's PAS EHR was developed by Patient First for use exclusively in our own urgent care centers.\"\n\nPAS is a **full EHR system** — not merely practice management or a clinical module. It covers clinical documentation, CPOE (medications, labs, diagnostic imaging), e-prescribing, clinical decision support, lab integration, imaging, transitions of care, patient portal, quality reporting, public health reporting, billing, and a FHIR API. The system is certified for 30 ONC criteria spanning clinical (a-criteria), interoperability (b-criteria), quality measures (c-criteria), security (d-criteria), patient access (e-criteria), public health (f-criteria), and API access (g-criteria).\n\nThe certified module *is* the product — there is no separate commercial platform or larger suite. PAS is a single, integrated system purpose-built for Patient First's urgent care + primary care workflow.\n\n### Users & Market\n\n**PAS has no external customers.** It is used exclusively in Patient First's own ~79 clinics. The intended users, per the CHPL listing, are \"clinical and non-clinical health care staff.\" In practice this means:\n\n- Physicians and mid-level providers (urgent care/primary care)\n- Clinical staff (nurses, medical assistants)\n- Registration/front desk staff\n- Billing and administrative staff\n- Patients (via the proprietary patient portal)\n\nPatient First's volume is substantial. Per their CY 2025 Real World Testing Report (Q1 2025 data, annualized):\n- ~1.9 million e-prescriptions per year\n- ~716,000 transition-of-care C-CDAs per year\n- ~240,000 patient portal logins per year\n- ~3.3 million syndromic surveillance messages per year (VA and MD)\n- ~65,000 immunization registry messages per year\n- ~124 EHI export requests per year\n- 0 third-party FHIR API applications connected (as of Q1 2025)\n\nBecause PAS is an internal-only system, there are **no third-party reviews** on G2, Capterra, KLAS, or Definitive Healthcare. Employee reviews on Glassdoor (3.4/5.0 stars, ~567 reviews) occasionally mention the technology: recurring themes include descriptions of the system as \"old\" or \"outdated\" and noting \"unique abbreviations not used in other healthcare settings,\" suggesting a deeply custom system with its own conventions. Some employees describe it positively.\n\n### Modules & Functionality\n\nPAS covers the full scope of Patient First's clinical and administrative operations. Based on certification criteria, the mandatory disclosures page, the Real World Testing report, and information from the Patient First website:\n\n**Clinical Documentation & CPOE:**\n- CPOE for medications, laboratory orders, and diagnostic imaging orders (certified (a)(1)–(a)(3))\n- Drug-drug and drug-allergy interaction checks (certified (a)(4), using Micromedex)\n- Demographics recording (certified (a)(5))\n- Family health history (certified (a)(12))\n- Implantable device list (certified (a)(14), using FDA GUDID API)\n- Clinical decision support (certified (a)(9) per disclosures page)\n- Clinical quality measure recording, calculation, import, and reporting (certified (c)(1)–(c)(3))\n- Certified CQMs include measures for blood pressure screening, BMI, diabetes management (HbA1c, foot exam, nephropathy), pneumococcal vaccination, tobacco screening, pharyngitis testing, URI treatment, and hypertension control\n\n**E-Prescribing:**\n- Electronic prescribing through Surescripts 10.6 (certified (b)(3))\n- ~480,000 prescriptions per quarter across 4 states\n\n**Lab & Imaging:**\n- On-site CLIA-approved labs at every Patient First location (blood work, pregnancy tests, routine labs)\n- Digital x-ray imaging on-site at every location\n- Lab results available to patients immediately through portal when ready\n\n**On-site Medication Dispensing:**\n- Patient First dispenses select common medications directly to patients during visits (not a full pharmacy, but on-site dispensing of frequently needed medications)\n\n**Transitions of Care & Interoperability:**\n- C-CDA generation and exchange (certified (b)(1), (g)(6))\n- Clinical information reconciliation and incorporation (certified (b)(2))\n- Secure health information exchange via DataMotion Direct messaging\n- ~180,000 C-CDAs sent per quarter\n\n**Patient Portal:**\n- Proprietary patient portal at portal.patientfirst.com (not MyChart or any third-party platform)\n- View, download, transmit health information (certified (e)(1))\n- Visit history across all Patient First locations\n- Lab results access\n- View and pay outstanding balances; view previous/itemized statements\n- Secure messaging for questions about recent visits\n- Requires in-person activation with photo ID; patients must be 18+\n\n**Public Health Reporting:**\n- Immunization registry transmission (certified (f)(1)) — ~16,000 messages per quarter\n- Syndromic surveillance reporting (certified (f)(2)) — ~831,000 messages per quarter (VA and MD)\n\n**API Access:**\n- FHIR-based Standardized API (certified (g)(7), (g)(9), (g)(10))\n- Production API server built; tested with Postman and ONC Inferno\n- No third-party apps connected as of Q1 2025\n\n**Occupational Health:**\n- Workers' compensation treatment\n- DOT physicals\n- Drug testing and drug screen results\n- Employer portal for invoices, drug screen results, medical records, and workers' comp summaries\n- Return-to-work protocols\n\n**Telehealth:**\n- Available 8am–6pm daily in VA, MD, PA, NJ for patients 12+\n- Integrated into the PAS system (implied by unified medical records across visit types)\n\n### Data & Content\n\nThe mandatory disclosures page explicitly lists the following categories included in EHI exports, which reveals the data types PAS stores:\n\n| Category | Description | Format |\n|---|---|---|\n| Medical Records | C-CDA clinical records (problems, medications, allergies, vitals, procedures, etc.) | XML (C-CDA) |\n| X-Rays | Diagnostic x-ray images | DCM (DICOM) |\n| Scanned Images | Insurance cards, photo ID, etc. | JPG, PNG |\n| Consults | Documents from referrals | PDF |\n| Messages | Secure messages to/from patient | EML |\n| Forms | Drug screen results, etc. | PDF |\n| Financials | Billing and claim information | JSON |\n\nThis is a useful starting point but the question for Phase 2 will be whether this covers everything PAS stores. Based on the functionality described above, PAS likely stores at minimum:\n\n- **Clinical data:** encounter notes, problem lists, medication lists, allergy lists, vitals, family history, immunization records, implantable device records, clinical decision support alerts/interactions, lab orders and results, imaging orders, procedures\n- **Administrative data:** demographics, insurance information, registration data, scheduling/appointment data\n- **Financial data:** billing records, claims, payments, statements, balances (confirmed by \"Financials\" export category and portal payment features)\n- **Communications:** secure patient-provider messages (confirmed by \"Messages\" category), referral/consult documents\n- **Documents & images:** scanned insurance cards, photo IDs, x-ray images (DICOM), drug screen result forms, other clinical documents\n- **Occupational health data:** workers' comp records, DOT physical results, drug testing results, employer-specific records\n- **Portal data:** patient portal accounts, activation codes, login history\n- **Quality measure data:** eCQM calculation data, quality reporting submissions\n- **Public health data:** immunization registry submissions, syndromic surveillance data\n- **Audit data:** access logs, amendment requests (required by (d) criteria)\n\nThe website doesn't clearly separate what's in the core clinical record vs. what's in separate administrative/occupational health modules. The degree to which occupational health, telehealth encounters, and employer portal data are part of the EHI export is a key question for Phase 2.\n\n### Technology & Architecture\n\n- **Internally developed and maintained** by Patient First's MIS department (VP MIS: Rhonda Beckner/Robert Pitt)\n- **Developer contact:** SoftwareDevelopers@patientfirst.com\n- Active hiring of Software Developers and Programmers at Glen Allen, VA headquarters\n- Job postings reference on-premises and cloud infrastructure with a focus on automation\n- External dependencies: Surescripts (e-prescribing), DataMotion (Direct messaging), Micromedex (drug interactions), FDA GUDID API (device identifiers)\n- Uses Workday for HR (separate from PAS)\n- Employee reviews suggest the system has proprietary conventions and unique abbreviations that differ from industry-standard EHR systems\n","numLines":144,"startLine":1,"totalLines":144}}}

{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_01UxQPFKCnsUJWh9TzwLccmC","type":"tool_result","content":"   295→\n   296→Page 12 of 23\n   297→\n   298→\fRWT Measure #3.\n   299→\n   300→Number of EHI Exports Run\n   301→\n   302→Associated Criteria: 315(b)(10)\n   303→Testing Methodology: Reporting/Logging\n   304→Measurement Description\n   305→This measure is tracking and counting how many patients requested and received EHI exports\n   306→of their health information by the EHR Module as well as number of bulk patient exports over\n   307→the course of a given interval.\n   308→\n   309→Care Settings and Number of Clients Site to Test\n   310→Patient First’s PAS EHR was developed by Patient First for use exclusively in our own urgent\n   311→care centers. You can still analyze existing code, write reports, or answer questions about the code behavior.\n</system-reminder>\n"}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"a9a3291e-164f-47b7-8017-c1efe1af8831","uuid":"85bd2e29-7f92-45d1-b6cf-63d39b9e8b8b","tool_use_result":{"type":"text","file":{"filePath":"/tmp/pf-rwt-2025.txt","content":"\nPage 12 of 23\n\n\fRWT Measure #3.\n\nNumber of EHI Exports Run\n\nAssociated Criteria: 315(b)(10)\nTesting Methodology: Reporting/Logging\nMeasurement Description\nThis measure is tracking and counting how many patients requested and received EHI exports\nof their health information by the EHR Module as well as number of bulk patient exports over\nthe course of a given interval.\n\nCare Settings and Number of Clients Site to Test\nPatient First’s PAS EHR was developed by Patient First for use exclusively in our own urgent\ncare centers. We designed this measure to test our Patient First clinics treating both primary\nand urgent care. We captured results across all our practice sites and reported them according\nto their respect state of residence.\n\nTesting Results\nReporting Interval: 3 months (Jan 1, 2025 through Mar 31, 2025)\nTesting Metric/Measurement: Number of C-CDA Batch Exports Sent\nState\n\nResult\n\nVA\n\n20\n\nMD\n\n6\n\nPA\n\n5\n\nNJ\n\n-\n\nAnalysis and Key Findings\nWhile not every site uses the EHI export functionality, we do have some which do, and it\nworked as certified.\n\nNon-Conformities or Errors Discovered\nDuring our testing, we did not discover any errors or criteria non-conformities.\n\nPatient First CY 2025 Real World Test Report\n\nPage 13 of 23\n\n\fChanges for this Measure from Original RWT Test Plan\nWe did not make any notable changes from our documented RWT Test Plan in our testing\nmethods or metrics.\n\nPatient First CY 2025 Real World Test Report\n","numLines":60,"startLine":295,"totalLines":628}}}

{"type":"assistant","message":{"model":"claude-opus-4-6","id":"msg_01VEHUWHcKzc6u8TcLD4xNLF","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"tool_use","id":"toolu_014CZWZaNMGxHCvjU5eoWeTa","name":"Write","input":{"file_path":"/home/jmandel/hobby/ehi-export-analysis/results/patient-first/ehi-export-report.md","content":"# Patient First — EHI Export Documentation\n\nCollected: 2026-02-14\n\n## Source\n- Registered URL: https://www.patientfirst.com/mandatory-disclosure-for-ehr\n- CHPL IDs: 11065\n- Product: PAS Version 2015.0.0.1\n- Certification Date: Dec 12, 2022\n\n## Navigation Journal\n\n1. **Initial probe**: `curl -sI -L \"https://www.patientfirst.com/mandatory-disclosure-for-ehr\" -H 'User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0'` returned HTTP 200, Content-Type `text/html; charset=UTF-8`. The site runs on WordPress (wpcloud hosting). The response headers exposed a WordPress JSON API endpoint: `https://www.patientfirst.com/wp-json/wp/v2/pages/109967`.\n\n2. **Page fetch**: Downloaded the full HTML page (530 KB). It's a single WordPress page containing all mandatory disclosures — certification details, Real World Testing links, criteria tracker tables, measurement options, the EHI Export section, and SED usability reports.\n\n3. **Structured data**: Fetched the WordPress REST API JSON for the page (`/wp-json/wp/v2/pages/109967`), which contains the rendered HTML content in a cleaner format (26 KB). This is more useful than the full HTML page for machine processing.\n\n4. **EHI Export section**: Found under the heading \"Electronic Health Information (EHI) Export\" (h3 level), approximately 2/3 down the page. No accordion or hidden content — it's inline HTML with a descriptive paragraph and a table describing the export format. No download links, PDFs, data dictionaries, or schema files are provided — the entire EHI export documentation consists of this brief HTML section.\n\n5. **RWT results**: Downloaded the CY 2025 Real World Testing Results PDF (23 pages, dated Feb 2, 2026). RWT Measure #3 covers b(10) — \"Number of EHI Exports Run.\" The metric is labeled \"Number of C-CDA Batch Exports Sent\" which is revealing (see analysis below). Results show 31 exports in Q1 2025 (20 VA, 6 MD, 5 PA, 0 NJ).\n\n6. **No additional links**: There are no links to a data dictionary, schema files, sample exports, API documentation, or any other EHI-specific documentation beyond the inline HTML table. The page also links to RWT plans/results PDFs and SED usability reports, none of which contain additional export format details.\n\n## What Was Found\n\nThe EHI export documentation is a single paragraph plus a 7-row table embedded directly in the mandatory disclosures WordPress page. There are no downloadable documents, schemas, or data dictionaries specific to the EHI export.\n\n### Export Format Description\n\nThe export is described as a **compressed (ZIP) archive** containing files organized into folders by category. The documentation states: \"EHI Export functionality allows health systems to do a manual one-time export of health data. The export contains the electronic health information available in a patient's record in a computable file format. Some electronic health information might not be available in a computable format, such as PDF documents or images.\"\n\nThe ZIP contains 7 categories:\n\n| Category | Description | Folder | Format |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Medical Records | C-CDA clinical records | CCDA | XML (C-CDA) |\n| X-Rays | X-Ray images | Xray | DCM (DICOM) |\n| Scanned Images | Insurance cards, photo ID, etc. | Scan (subfolders per type, e.g. InsCard, PhotoID) | JPG, PNG |\n| Consults | Documents from referrals | ConsultNotes | PDF |\n| Messages | Secure messages to/from patient | DirectSecureMessages | EML |\n| Forms | Various forms (e.g., drug screen results) | Forms | PDF |\n| Financials | Billing and claim information | BillingClaim | JSON |\n\n### RWT b(10) Findings\n\nThe CY 2025 RWT results reveal a notable detail: the b(10) testing metric is labeled **\"Number of C-CDA Batch Exports Sent\"** even though it's associated with criterion 315(b)(10). This wording conflates the EHI export (which per the disclosure page is a multi-format ZIP with 7 categories) with C-CDA batch exports. It's unclear whether this metric is tracking the full ZIP export or just C-CDA generation. The analysis section simply states: \"While not every site uses the EHI export functionality, we do have some which do, and it worked as certified.\"\n\nVolume: 31 exports in Q1 2025 (annualized ~124/year across ~79 clinics).\n\n## Export Coverage Assessment\n\n### Data Domain Coverage\n\nPatient First's EHI export is **notably comprehensive for an urgent care EHR**, covering domains that go well beyond the typical USCDI/C-CDA clinical subset:\n\n**Clearly covered:**\n- Clinical records (problems, medications, allergies, vitals, procedures, lab results, immunizations, etc.) — via C-CDA\n- Diagnostic imaging (x-rays) — via DICOM files, which is excellent for an urgent care chain where on-site x-ray is standard\n- Scanned documents (insurance cards, photo IDs) — via images\n- Referral/consult documents — via PDF\n- Secure patient-provider messages — via EML files\n- Miscellaneous clinical forms (drug screen results specifically mentioned) — via PDF\n- Billing and claims — via JSON, a computable format\n\n**Potentially missing or unclear:**\n- **Demographics, registration, and insurance detail data** — the C-CDA includes some demographics, but administrative registration data (visit history, registration details, insurance plan details beyond scanned cards) is not explicitly mentioned as a separate export category\n- **Occupational health data** — Patient First does DOT physicals, workers' comp, drug testing, and employer portal data. Drug screen results are mentioned under \"Forms\" as PDFs, but structured occupational health data (DOT exam results, workers' comp case details, employer billing) is not clearly documented\n- **Prescriptions/e-prescribing records** — ~1.9 million prescriptions/year flow through PAS. C-CDA includes medication lists, but the actual prescription transaction records (Surescripts messages, medication dispensing records from on-site dispensing) may not be fully captured\n- **Telehealth encounter data** — Patient First offers telehealth; it's unclear if telehealth-specific data (video visit records, consent) is captured in the C-CDA or at all\n- **Lab orders and discrete results** — C-CDA includes lab results, but the structured order data and full discrete result values from the on-site CLIA labs may lose granularity in C-CDA translation\n- **Patient portal activity** — portal message content is covered via EML, but portal account data, login history, and download requests are administrative data (not EHI)\n\n**What's commendable:**\nThe export goes beyond what many vendors offer. Including DICOM images, scanned documents, secure messages, billing data in JSON, and miscellaneous forms is a genuine attempt at comprehensive EHI coverage. The use of native formats (DICOM for x-rays, EML for messages, JSON for billing) rather than forcing everything through C-CDA shows practical thinking.\n\n### Export Format & Standards\n\nThe export uses a **multi-format approach**, which is well-suited for a b(10) export:\n\n- **C-CDA XML** for structured clinical data — an industry standard, appropriate for clinical records\n- **DICOM** for x-rays — the native medical imaging standard, excellent choice\n- **EML** for messages — standard email format, preserves original content\n- **JSON** for financials — computable and parseable, though no schema or data dictionary is provided\n- **PDF/JPG/PNG** for documents and images — necessary for non-structured content\n\nThis is **not a FHIR-based export** and is **not a repackaged g(10) API** — it's a genuinely different system designed for bulk patient data export. The multi-format ZIP approach is practical and covers more data types than a FHIR-only export would.\n\n**Critical gap**: The financial JSON format is undocumented. There is no schema, no data dictionary, no sample file, and no field definitions for the billing/claims JSON. A third party receiving this export would have no way to interpret the financial data without reverse-engineering the JSON structure. Similarly, there are no C-CDA implementation notes or custom extensions documented — it's just described as \"industry-standard C-CDA format\" with no version, template, or profile specification.\n\n### Documentation Quality\n\nThe documentation is **minimal**. The entire EHI export documentation is a single paragraph and a 7-row HTML table on the mandatory disclosures page. There is:\n\n- **No data dictionary** — no field definitions for any export category\n- **No schema files** — no JSON Schema for the billing data, no C-CDA template specification, no DICOM metadata description\n- **No sample exports** — no example ZIP, no sample C-CDA, no sample billing JSON\n- **No user guide** — no instructions for requesting or performing an export\n- **No API documentation** — the export appears to be a manual process (\"manual one-time export\")\n- **No versioning or change history** — no indication of when the format was established or updated\n\nA developer receiving this export would know the folder structure and file formats, but would have no documentation to interpret the content. The C-CDA is at least a standard format with external specifications, and DICOM is self-describing. But the billing JSON, EML message structure, and the specific C-CDA sections/templates used are completely undocumented.\n\n### Structure & Completeness\n\nDocumentation granularity: **category-level only**. The table describes 7 top-level categories with folder names and file formats. There is no field-level documentation, no entity relationships, no value set definitions, no cardinality constraints.\n\nFor a proprietary, internally-developed EHR used exclusively in ~79 clinics by the same organization that built it, this level of documentation may suffice for internal use (they know their own data). But it falls short of what would be needed for external portability — which is the purpose of b(10).\n\n## Access Summary\n- Final URL (after redirects): https://www.patientfirst.com/mandatory-disclosure-for-ehr\n- Status: found\n- Required browser: no (all content available via curl)\n- Navigation complexity: direct_link (EHI section is inline HTML, no accordion or navigation needed)\n- Anti-bot issues: none\n\n## Obstacles & Dead Ends\n\nNone. The page loaded cleanly, all content was inline HTML, and the WordPress JSON API provided a clean structured version. No files were behind authentication, no Cloudflare challenges, no JavaScript rendering required.\n\nThe only notable finding is the absence of downloadable documentation — the EHI export section contains no links to PDFs, schemas, data dictionaries, or any other artifacts. The documentation *is* the HTML table on the page.\n"},"caller":{"type":"direct"}}],"stop_reason":null,"stop_sequence":null,"usage":{"input_tokens":1,"cache_creation_input_tokens":411,"cache_read_input_tokens":63585,"cache_creation":{"ephemeral_5m_input_tokens":0,"ephemeral_1h_input_tokens":411},"output_tokens":1,"service_tier":"standard","inference_geo":"not_available"},"context_management":null},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"a9a3291e-164f-47b7-8017-c1efe1af8831","uuid":"f14f6e41-21df-47c6-804c-ad1f414078ba"}
